sections.text: Let him hold body, head and neck erect, motionless and steady; let him look fixedly at the tip of his nose, turning neither to the right nor to the left.
With peace in his heart and no fear, observing the vow of celibacy, with mind controlled and fixed on Me, let the student lose himself in contemplation of Me.
Thus keeping his mind always in communion with Me, and with his thoughts subdued, he shall attain that Peace which is mine and which will lead him to liberation at last.

Unlike a car with its users manual, we are born without instructions how to live. We experience life vicissitudes without a so called users manual. The Gita has been described as such a guide.
We had been discussing chapter six, Dhyana Yoga Yoga of Meditation. We have so far understood that the yogi is trying to achieve a state of mind where he is not attached to either the sense objects or his actions, and he does not have any grand plans for the future. To achieve this state of mind, one obviously has to turn ones gaze to the inner self and stop letting the mind run out to the outer world.
The nature of the mind is obviously to go after the sense objects because it is receiving the information from the senses, senses, reports to the mind. And mind wants to go out and analyze those experiences in the world of sense objects. For this mind to train to turn inward is the training of meditation.
And we have seen that Bhagavan has given a clear instruction of how to start this practice. Obviously anything which we are doing and we want to change it, you have to make it a practice, a habit. I heard somewhere that if you do something seven times, it becomes a habit.
And I have personally experienced that if I get up one day at 6:30 and it seems too early the next day, I try a little harder and still get up at 6:30. And then after a while that becomes my normal routine that Ill get up at 6:30. So the mind gradually gets used to what we do in a routine manner, or we do it repeatedly.
My mind is a flow of thoughts. In whatever direction we turn it, thats the direction the mind will start flowing into. Right now the mind has been trained since my birth to go out to the outside world and gather information whether that experience is conducive or not conducive, whether it is a pleasant or unpleasant experience.
And my happiness or unhappiness right now is defined by my experiences which are either conducive or unconducive, pleasant or unpleasant. Dhyana Yoga is the practice to turn this mind away from this outer experiences and experience the inner self. So so far we have seen that the instruction is given that having lived the life of a selfless activity.
In other words, I have now changed my priorities in my life. Where whatever Im doing, I will be thinking about the greater good. Then I will think about not only practicing this art for making money or making my living, but also how good I can make the others lives.
My clients will be using these buildings. Whether have I improved their lives. And that will be my motivation in practicing my art.
If I train my mind to think that way for everything I do, my activities start becoming more selfless than selfish. More and more I practice my selfless activities. My mind becomes purer and purer and seeing the world outside.
But I have yet not trained itself to turn inward to see what is the experience of myself. And thats where the meditation come in place. So the instruction we have seen in last few _Verses_ it says such.
Establish a place of your own meditation which is steady and firm. Naati uchritam naati nicham that it is not too tall, not too low. And once Ive established my place of meditation, Ive become comfortable on that asana.
And I sit down with my folded legs or any other position which is most comfortable. The whole goal is to make my body so comfortable that my mind does not run towards discomfort of my body. My mind gets used to sitting at that place and realizing that now is the time to contemplate and meditate.
Im training my mind. Im programming my mind that once I sit down at this place, it is time to meditate. So the next instruction was, what do I do once I sit down? I sit down, I close my eyes lightly.
And then the instructions say tatra ekagramana kutva. Then focusing the mind at a single point, Yatachatta indriya kriyah. That controlling the senses.
Im not letting my eyes to see, my ears to hear, or my skin to feel any touch. And I will be practicing this for the purpose of atma vishuddaye, for purifying my internal instrument. I keep this goal in mind at the seat of meditation.
That I am doing this for my internal the purification of my internal instrument. Antakarana, my mind and intellect, the operating system of myself, which is my mind and intellect. So the next three _Verses_ gives us further instructions into what would be the most appropriate posture to achieve that.
So the verse 13 says, Samam kaya shirogrivam dharayan achalam sthiraha. I sat down, I closed my eyes, but Im trying to focus my mind and I feel the weight of my body. Its slouching me down and slumping me down and that distracts me.
I have never understood this before. I joined Chinmaya Mission and started hearing and learning about meditation. But I heard ing that the most comfortable position will be to sit erect.
If you want to sit at the seat of meditation, not only that you have to have a right, right seat, but you have to right posture so that you can sit without any stress and strain or having any discomfort in your body in the posture which is most natural, most natural posture. I now understand this as an architectural principle: if I have a straight column, it will have less stress because Im transferring all the load on that column straight down to the earth. But if I have a bent column with a load on the second floor at the top of it, that column will have more stress and strain.
And I have to design it in a way that it has more reinforcement and all different type of calculations to make sure that the column remains in place. Its a simple fact in structural knowledge: if I have a straight column, it requires less strength because there is less strain from the load imposed on it. This actually applies to our body too, because our body is nothing but a structure, just like any building.
When we are sitting down and our backbone is bent, it puts more stress on it to keep itself in place. That stress and strain eventually transfers to my mind, which starts thinking about how to become comfortable. So I need to create a posture which is the most natural in nature is to have a straight column.
My backbone should be completely straight. So therefore it says Samam kaya shira grivam. Keep the head, neck and the body in a straight line.
Its an observation by our rishis that this is the most comfortable position for our self, our body. It will less strain if you work on your posture and all the time make sure that you are sitting straight. You will realize it is the most comfortable position, and you can sit in it for a longer period without feeling any stress on your body.
This comes straight from Bhagavad Gita: Samam Kaya Shirogrivam -- having your body, neck, and head in a straight line. Dharayan Achalam -- hold it without moving. Once again, lets go back to my own architectural training.
If I have a column with wind load applied on it and it is moving in the wind -- I learned to my surprise when I started working on high-rise buildings that all high-rise buildings actually sway in the wind, just like a tree moves in the wind. We typically think the buildings are stable and they dont move. But all buildings move just like a tree would move in a wind.
So in a high rise building which are about 50, 60, 70 stories tall or more, they literally move in a wind just like a tree would move. And I even have heard that people get seasickness on the, on the top floors of high rise, those who are very, very sensitive to movement. Because at the top floor, if you are in a hundred story building or 110 story building and you are on a 110th floor, the movement may be in feet.
You know, the building moves several feet from one side to another. And people who are sensitive, most people dont, may not feel it. But some people who are very sensitive start feeling their movement, they develop something similar to seasickness.
So if the column is straight, no other force is applied on it, and its not moving, it has the least stress. But on a high-rise building that will move in the wind, the engineer has to calculate that movement and design for those forces so the column remains steady under wind load. He has to add more reinforcement and strength to keep this column intact under those conditions.
So once more: our backbone, when it is moving, experiences more stress and strain, and eventually that transfers to our mind. If I want my mind completely relieved of any disturbance, I need to relieve it from any stress coming from my body. So Bhagavan says Dharayan Achalam -- hold this posture of having the head, neck, and body in a straight line, firmly, without moving.
That does not mean a stiff posture where Im trying not to move, but naturally achieving that firmness in a most relaxed manner. Now I have the seat, Ive sat down on it, Ive held my body in a firm position, my posture is corrected, my backbone is completely straight. How do I control my mind? At one point Ill have to give my mind something to think about, something to focus on.
The next line says: Samprekshya nasikagram svam -- gaze at your own nose tip. Somebody will say, But Rajan, my eyes are closed. How am I going to gaze at my nose tip? Well, youre not really seeing; you are trying to focus on it.
With your eyes closed, focus your mind at the tip of your nose. You are not seeing it, you are imagining it. Focusing your mind at the tip of your nose.
Dishash cha anavalokayan -- without seeing in the other directions. Our mind has a very imaginative nature. When you close your eyes, the first thing the mind does is, Well, I cant see now, but let me imagine whats around me.
What if I look to the right? What must be happening? Would I look on the left? What must be happening? What could be behind me and what could be ahead of me? This nature of imagining things, we need to stop my mind to do. Therefore Im trying to focus my mind at the tip of my nose and not letting it go in all other direction. So the verse 13 has told us how to sit erect, hold the body firm then gaze at the tip of your nose with your eyes lightly closed and not let the mind try to imagine whats on the other side.
In the next verse say this.

The instruction samam kaya-shiro-grivam - keep the body, head, and neck in a straight line - contains profound structural wisdom. Just as a straight column in a building carries weight with minimum stress while a bent column requires extra reinforcement, your spine when erect allows you to sit for extended periods without strain. The body becomes so comfortable that the mind forgets it, freeing attention for the inward journey. This is not rigid stiffness but natural alignment - relaxed yet upright.
The practice of gazing at the nose tip with eyes gently closed addresses our minds imaginative nature. With eyes closed, the mind immediately begins constructing images: What is happening on my left? What is behind me? By focusing attention on a single point - the nose tip - we give the restless mind an anchor, preventing it from wandering in all directions. The instruction dishash cha anavalokayan - not looking in various directions - applies to mental wandering, not just physical seeing.
The promise of verse 15 is extraordinary: Shantim nirvana-paramam mat-samstham adhigacchati - the yogi attains supreme peace that resides in Me. This peace we seek so desperately in the external world simply does not exist there. It is like riding a roller coaster and wishing it would stabilize - the nature of the roller coaster is movement. True stability is found only by stepping off onto solid ground. Today, practice sitting in correct posture for just five minutes, focusing on the breath at the tip of your nose, gently returning when the mind wanders. This small practice, done consistently, is the doorway to that supreme peace.
